1:
Whether the Amalekite’s story is true at all divides them four ways. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) rejects it entire: the whole account is a fabrication, grossly self-contradictory in many of its particulars, and there is no fact in the case but the bringing of the crown and bracelets, which a plunderer of the slain had found on the field and carried to David with a lie attached to ingratiate himself. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) keeps the facts and discards the role: the man reports the defeat and the deaths as they really occurred, but it is uncertain whether he saw Saul at all before his death, and extremely unlikely that he found him wounded and alone, without warriors or armour-bearer. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) will not decide, saying plainly that he is not clear whether the story was true, and offering a harmonisation if it was — what the earlier narrative calls a sword may here be called a spear, or in falling on his sword he leaned on his spear.

The doubt is pressed on particular words. John Gill (reformed) fixes on the request itself, which he can hardly think Saul would have made, since the king might as well have died by the hands of the uncircumcised Philistines, which he had been labouring to avoid, as by the hand of an Amalekite. Ellicott questions even the man’s presence in the army, observing that nobody unconcerned in the matter is likely to stray into the middle of a battle, so that the phrase about chance is better referred to his coming upon the wounded king than to his being on the mountain; yet he grants that the man certainly claims to have belonged to the camp of Israel. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) gloss the king’s complaint itself as a cramp, on the rabbinic explanation, which had left him unable to defend himself and certain to fall into Philistine hands. Henry notes that those who would rejoice at the fall of an enemy are apt to measure others by themselves and to expect the same welcome, which is why the tale was told as it was.

What the obeisance meant is agreed, and what it earned is not what he expected. Ellicott takes it for no mere act of Oriental respect but a deliberate recognition of David’s rank as having now become king, noting that the earth on his head and his rent clothes were marks of sorrow for the defeat of David’s people and the death of their king. Henry turns it to irony: the man pleased himself with the fancy that he had the honour to be first to do homage to his sovereign, and proved to be the first to receive sentence of death from his judge, not doubting that his officiousness would recommend him to the best preferments in the camp.

That the crown came by an Amalekite’s hand is read as justice. Henry observes the righteousness of it, that Saul, who had spared the Amalekites in contempt of the divine command, took his death-wound from one, and that where Saul had spared the best of their spoil the best of his now came to one of that devoted nation. Clarke reaches the same thought by another road, reporting the remark that an Amalekite took from Saul’s head the crown he had forfeited by his disobedience in the matter of Amalek. Ellicott supplies the long enmity behind it, the Amalekites having attacked Israel on their first coming out of Egypt and repeatedly after, and having been terribly defeated by Saul himself, so that this man had perhaps attached himself to the conqueror’s army or been compelled by ancient custom to serve in its ranks. On the rabbinic tradition that he was Doeg’s son both Henry and Gill are dismissive, Henry calling it a groundless conceit.
11:
The grief is taken to be real, and the point is pressed. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) allows no doubt of it: though David had just heard of the death of his persistent and mortal enemy and of his own consequent accession, there is not the slightest reason to question the reality and earnestness of his mourning, since the narrative shows a personal attachment to Saul notwithstanding that long and unreasonable hostility — and he adds the observation that, the men of Jabesh-gilead excepted, the only deep mourning for Saul came from the man he had hated and persecuted as long as he lived. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) marks how far the event fell out from what the messenger expected, a passion of weeping where a transport of joy was looked for, and mourning not only for Israel and for Jonathan his friend but for Saul his enemy; he did it as a man of honour, by that decorum which forbids us to insult over the fallen, and as a man of conscience who had forgiven the injuries done him.

Ellicott separates the grounds of the sorrow, that besides his personal loss David had a religious and a patriotic cause, the fallen being parts of that Church of God which he so earnestly loved and served and also members of the commonwealth of Israel on whose behalf he ever laboured; and he judges that the Septuagint, overlooking the distinction, has very unnecessarily altered the people of the Lord into the people of Judah. Henry turns the mourning to a further use, arguing that it shows what temper lay behind those passages in the psalms which express a desire for the ruin of enemies: they proceeded not from a spirit of revenge but from a holy zeal for the glory of God and the public good, since a man whose natural temper was this tender was kindly affected even to those who hated him.

That the man was judged out of his own mouth is the one point on which all agree, and each arrives at it differently. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) put the reasoning most fully: he is judged by his own testimony whether he did the deed or not, for if he did he receives the just reward of it, and if he did not he must throw the blame on his own lying witness and be content with the wages of a wicked flatterer. Ellicott reaches the same ground in a sentence, that it does not matter whether David fully believed the story, the man being judged by his own account of himself. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) concedes it even while holding the tale a fabrication, since at that time nothing was known to the contrary and the man was executed upon his own confession.

Why regicide was so grave, and what the words imply, are handled separately. Ellicott insists it was no mere political crime in David’s eyes, who had shown on more than one occasion of great temptation that he held the taking of the Lord’s anointed to be a religious offence of the greatest magnitude, and especially grievous in a foreigner; he also sets aside any question of David’s authority to pass a capital sentence, the man having just recognised him as king and so acknowledged it. John Gill (reformed) draws an inference from the reproach itself, that to stretch forth the hand must mean more than standing on the body and pressing it so the spear might pierce through, but that he drew his sword and slew him, which is how David understood it; and on the question whence he came Gill reports Abarbinel’s view that it asked neither place nor nation but whose servant he was.
17:
Whether David taught Judah a weapon or a song is a straight division. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) argues for the song and argues it at length: the words rendered as the use of are not in the Hebrew, and Kasheth is the title of the dirge that follows, as many of the psalms carry such titles, named the Bow because the defeat was the work of Philistine archers and still more for the sake of Jonathan’s bow, which returned not from the blood of the slain; he has David commit the teaching of it to the chief musicians. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) agrees that the italicised words should be omitted and the dirge be called the bow, both from that allusion and because it is a martial ode, adding that it was taught to Judah rather than to all Israel because David reigned over Judah and Benjamin alone for the next seven years and a half.

The other two take it for arms drill. John Gill (reformed) puts the clause in a parenthesis as no part of the elegy at all, inserted to show that amid his sorrow David was not unmindful of his people’s defence but would have them trained in military exercises, the bow standing for every weapon and named the rather because the Philistines were expert with it — said indeed to be its inventors, though Gill notes that Pliny ascribes it to others. John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) makes Judah the particular object of the order as the chief and now royal tribe, bordering on Philistia and likely to prove the bulwark of all Israel. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) sets out both readings and declines to settle between them, observing only that the men of Judah had lately made more use of slings, and that it was the Philistine archers who bore so hard upon Saul.

On the book it was written in, and what kind of composition it is, they go further than the verse. Clarke collects the versions, which make it the book of the upright, or the book of the Law, or on the Arabic the book of Samuel. Ellicott says that nothing more is really known of it for all the endless discussion, supposing it a collection of songs on early Israel’s memorable men and events. Henry takes it for a collection of state poems long since lost, and draws from the fact of its being lodged there a conclusion the others do not reach: the elegy is no divine hymn given by inspiration for use in divine service, there being no mention of God in it from end to end, but a human composition, and so was set down in Jasher and not among the psalms.

That the embargo on the news is a wish and not a command is agreed by three. Gill says David could not hinder the victory being known and talked of at Gath, so the words are not a command but a wish that it were not so. Wesley makes the same distinction a rule, that this is no precept but a poetical wish, expressing not a desire for what he knew to be impossible but his great sorrow that it would be done, to the dishonour of God and his people. Henry calls it an embargo he would fain lay upon Fame, and finds the sting of it in memory: the Philistines would the more insult because Israel had once sung that Saul had slain his thousands, and that song would now be retorted. Ellicott adds that the two cities stand poetically for the whole country, and that the phrase appears to have passed into a proverb. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) explain the daughters by the custom of employing women to celebrate a nation’s victories with singing and dancing.
22:
The two weapons are read as a figure, and divided between the two men. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) take the passage to rest on the image of arrows that drink the blood of the enemy and a sword that devours their flesh, and note that the principal weapons are apportioned between the pair, the bow to Jonathan and the sword to Saul; the ignominy on Gilboa was the greater in men whose bow and sword had never turned back until satisfied. John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) reaches the same figure by the grammar, that the sword is metaphorically said to have a mouth, which we translate an edge, and to devour, so that it returned not empty but filled and glutted; and he adds that their former success is mentioned here as an aggravation of their last infelicity. John Gill (reformed) reads it of unfailing execution, the arrows always piercing and bringing down the mighty, and compares the arrows of the Medes and Persians, which are said not to return in vain.

How much of lovely and pleasant can be said of Saul is handled with care by all of them. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) allows that it belongs peculiarly to Jonathan but in a good degree to Saul in his earlier years and better moments, which David chose at this moment to recall. Keil and Delitzsch say the same of the two predicates, that they apply chiefly to Jonathan though they suited Saul in the earliest years of his reign, when he showed the virtues of an able ruler; and they admire that the noble Jonathan did not forsake his father, whose fierce hatred of the friend Jonathan loved as his own soul might well have undermined that attachment.

What the praise leaves out is noticed twice over. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) observes that David does not commend Saul for what he was not and says nothing of his piety or fidelity, since funeral commendations gathered out of the spoils of truth are no praise to those on whom they are bestowed but very much the dispraise of those who misplace them. Wesley makes the same observation and turns it into a rule, that David speaks not a word of Saul’s piety but commends him only for the things that were truly in him, which he calls a fit pattern for all preachers in their funeral commendations. On the scarlet, Ellicott takes it of Saul’s division of the spoil of conquered foes and judges that, for all the cloud he went out under, he had on the whole been a successful warrior who bettered Israel’s standing among the nations. Henry puts the same prosperity more drily: when they had a king like the nations they must have clothes like the nations.

The friendship is weighed last. Henry finds the wonder of it in its object, that a man should love one whom he knew was to take the crown over his head and be so faithful to his rival, which far surpassed the highest degree of conjugal affection. Keil and Delitzsch read the comparison as expressive of the deepest earnestness of devoted love, and gloss the word for distress as the pinching of the heart that follows pain and mourning. Gill draws the finest distinction of the four: David was distressed for Jonathan not on account of his spiritual and eternal state, which he doubted not was happy, but for the manner of his death, the loss of him, and the want of his pleasant conversation and of his counsel in present circumstances. Of the closing line Keil and Delitzsch note that the instruments of war which perished are not the weapons themselves but a figure, and that this third strophe is only a brief aftertone in which the ode dies away.
